content: Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer affecting women globally, with approximately 569,847 new cases and 311,365 deaths annually. The incidence and stage at diagnosis vary significantly across different regions, largely influenced by the availability of effective population-based screening programs. For instance, in Nigeria, 86% to 89.3% of new cases are diagnosed at an advanced stage, whereas in the UK, only 21.9% of women present with stage II or higher disease according to the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) classification. Women with advanced cervical cancer frequently experience distressing symptoms, such as vaginal bleeding, which can be life-threatening. The incidence of vaginal bleeding in advanced cervical cancer ranges from 0.7% to 100%, and it is the immediate cause of death in 6% of affected women. Managing this bleeding is often challenging, making it a common and critical consequence of advanced disease. Despite its prevalence, there is currently no systematic review addressing palliative interventions specifically aimed at controlling vaginal bleeding in advanced cervical cancer. A comprehensive evaluation of available palliative treatments is necessary to guide clinical decision-making. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of various interventions, including tranexamic acid, vaginal packing (with or without formalin-soaked packs), interventional radiology, and other methods, compared to radiotherapy for the palliative management of vaginal bleeding in women with advanced cervical cancer. The original search for this review was conducted on March 23, 2015, with an updated search performed on March 21, 2018. Databases searched included the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and Embase. Additional sources included clinical trial registries, abstracts from scientific meetings, reference lists of review articles, and consultations with experts in the field. Citation lists of relevant studies were also manually reviewed. The inclusion criteria focused on randomised and non-randomised comparative studies evaluating the efficacy and safety of the aforementioned interventions compared to radiotherapy for palliative treatment of vaginal bleeding in women with advanced cervical cancer, regardless of publication status, year, or language. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies. However, no studies met the inclusion criteria, and no data were available for analysis. Of the 1522 unique references identified, 1330 were excluded based on title and abstract screening. The remaining 22 full-text articles were reviewed, but none satisfied the inclusion criteria. Only observational data from single-arm studies involving formalin-soaked packs, interventional radiology, or radiotherapy techniques were identified. The authors concluded that since the last version of this review, no new studies have been found. There is no evidence from controlled trials to either support or refute the use of any of the proposed interventions compared to radiotherapy. Consequently, the choice of intervention is likely to depend on the resources available locally. Radiotherapy, a common method for managing vaginal bleeding, is often inaccessible in resource-limited settings, where advanced cervical cancer is more prevalent. This review highlights the urgent need for a randomised controlled trial to evaluate the benefits and risks of palliative treatments for vaginal bleeding in women with advanced cervical cancer.
